Elamipretide (SS-31) Explained: The Mitochondria-Targeting Peptide and Its Side Effects

Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. Elamipretide (SS-31) Explained: The Mitochondria-Targeting Peptide and Its Side Effects

Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. In September 2025 the FDA granted it accelerated approval as Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome. This short covers how it works, what the TAZPOWER trial and its long-term extension showed, the mixed results in mitochondrial myopathy and dry macular degeneration, where the confirmatory and phase 3 trials stand, and what studies reported on side effects, from injection site reactions to allergic reactions and eosinophil changes. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #elamipretide #mitochondria #peptides

Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. In September 2025 the FDA granted it accelerated approval as Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome. This short covers how it works, what the TAZPOWER trial and its long-term extension showed, the mixed results in mitochondrial myopathy and dry macular degeneration, where the confirmatory and phase 3 trials stand, and what studies reported on side effects, from injection site reactions to allergic reactions and eosinophil changes. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #elamipretide #mitochondria #peptides

We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. Elamipretide (SS-31) Explained: The Mitochondria-Targeting Peptide and Its Side Effects

Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. In September 2025 the FDA granted it accelerated approval as Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome. This short covers how it works, what the TAZPOWER trial and its long-term extension showed, the mixed results in mitochondrial myopathy and dry macular degeneration, where the confirmatory and phase 3 trials stand, and what studies reported on side effects, from injection site reactions to allergic reactions and eosinophil changes. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. La cerimonia del rapè

🌿 PERCHÉ IL RAPÈ? Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Survodutide is not an FDA-approved drug. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #survodutide #GLP1 #peptides

We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. Peptide science without the hype. ⚠️ Educational and informational purposes only. Not medical advice. embedding_text:
GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. Peptide science without the hype. ⚠️ Educational and informational purposes only. Not medical advice. CJC-1295 is not FDA-approved for anti-aging, muscle building, or fat loss. #CJC1295 #Peptides #GrowthHormone #PeptideResearch #IGF1 ⚠️ DISCLAIMER This video is for educational purposes only. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? embedding_text:
CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. Peptide science without the hype. ⚠️ Educational and informational purposes only. Not medical advice. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance?
